MisleadQA: Diagnosing LLM Failures under Misleading Context

Hui Wang     Bohao Chu     Qianli Wang Affiliation: University of Duisburg-Essen Affiliation: Technische Universität Berlin Affiliation: Equal contribution.     *Correspondence: hw1361376751@gmail.com    Shuning Zhang     Norbert Fuhr Affiliation: University of Duisburg-Essen Affiliation: Tsinghua University
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer questions from retrieved or user-provided context. However, provided context can be factually true yet out-of-scope, describing a different entity, time, or location from the one the question targets, and still lead models to a wrong answer. Prior work has mainly studied factually false or irrelevant context. It remains unclear whether such out-of-scope context misleads models as much as false context, and whether adding gold context prevents models from being misled by either. We introduce MisleadQA, a diagnostic dataset of multiple-choice questions with an abstention option. Each question pairs gold context (G) with true but out-of-scope context (S) and false but in-scope context (F) supporting the same wrong answer. We evaluate six open-weight LLMs. On questions they answer correctly without context, providing S alone leads them to switch to this wrong answer in 29.3% of cases, and providing F alone does so in 75.4%. Adding G nearly removes the effect of S, but F still misleads models in 21.0% of cases, especially when F comes first. A context-faithful instruction reduces these errors mainly through abstention and lowers accuracy even with G. These findings suggest that evaluations should check whether context applies to the question, not only whether it is true, and should report correct, misled, and abstention rates together. Data and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MisleadQA.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer questions from context that is retrieved or user-provided (Lewis et al., 2020; Ram et al., 2023; Chu et al., 2026). To support the correct answer, the context must meet two conditions. It must be true (factual validity), and it must match the scope the question asks about, such as its entity, time, or location (scope applicability). Context may meet the first condition but fail the second. For example, it may correctly state a fact for a different year than the one asked about. We call such context out-of-scope. It points to a wrong answer without making any false claims (Figure 1). A model must therefore check not only whether the context is true but also whether it applies to the question.

Prior work shows that models can be misled by factually false or counterfactual context (Longpre et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024), and even by irrelevant context (Shi et al., 2023). Out-of-scope context lies between these cases: unlike false context, it is factually true, and unlike irrelevant context, it is closely related to the question. Some studies include such context (Chen et al., 2024; Amiraz et al., 2025; Shafiei et al., 2026), but none of them compares it with false context that supports the same wrong answer while keeping the question fixed (§2). It therefore remains unclear whether out-of-scope context misleads models as much as false context does, and whether adding gold context protects models against either.

Answering these questions requires true context that does not apply to the question, and false context to compare it with. We therefore introduce MisleadQA, a dataset of 959 multiple-choice questions with an abstention option, built from Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED)11 1 https://fred.stlouisfed.org/, accessed Oct 7, 2026., SituatedQA (Zhang and Choi, 2021), and AmbigDocs (Lee et al., 2024). Each question has a target scope and three contexts. Gold context (G) states the correct answer. True but out-of-scope context (S) states a true fact about a different entity, time, or location, like near-miss context from retrieval. False but in-scope context (F) assigns the value from S to the target scope. S and F thus support the same wrong answer, the lure, with everything else fixed. This lets us test whether S misleads models as much as F. Since S and F differ in both truth and scope, the comparison does not separate them.

We then conduct a diagnostic evaluation of six open-weight LLMs on MisleadQA, testing S and F alone and together with G, in both orders. To measure how context changes answers that models would otherwise get right, we focus on questions each model answers correctly without any context. On these questions, providing S alone leads models to switch to the lure in 29.3% of cases, and providing F alone does so even more often, in 75.4%. When G is added, such erroneous switches drop to 0.9% for S but remain at 21.0% for F.22 2 Rates are averaged equally across models. Rates with G average both orders unless stated otherwise, and use the questions also answered correctly with G alone, which include over 99% of the questions above (§4.2). Order matters mainly for F. When F is presented before G, erroneous switches rise sharply to 38.1%, compared with only 3.9% when G comes first.

We further analyze why S may mislead models and whether a context-faithful instruction can help. One possible reason is that models fail to notice the scope mismatch. To test this, we ask models in a separate task whether S applies to the question, using a 200-question subset. They judge only 62.4% of S contexts as out-of-scope, even though S states its scope explicitly. However, a correct judgment does not ensure a correct answer. Even when models judge S correctly, they still choose the lure on 20.3% of these questions when given S alone. We also test a context-faithful instruction, which tells models to use only applicable context and to abstain otherwise. It roughly halves lure selection under S, but mainly because models abstain far more often. It also lowers accuracy even when G is present. These results show that lower lure rates alone can hide a loss of correct answers, so evaluations of context-grounded question answering should report correct, misled, and abstention rates together. Overall, our contributions are:

  • •

    We construct MisleadQA, a dataset that pairs true but out-of-scope context with matched false context, keeping the question, options, wrong answer, and gold context fixed (§3).

  • •

    We perform a diagnostic evaluation of six open-weight LLMs (§4), showing that out-of-scope context alone often misleads models, and that adding gold context removes most of these errors but not those caused by false context, especially when the false context comes first (§5).

  • •

    We conduct targeted analyses, showing that models often fail to recognize S as out-of-scope and can still choose the lure even when they do, and that a context-faithful instruction reduces lure selection mainly through abstention while lowering accuracy when G is present (§6).

2 Related Work

Context-grounded question answering. LLMs often answer questions using context that is either retrieved from an external source (Lewis et al., 2020; Ram et al., 2023) or provided directly by the user Chu et al. (2025). Such context may conflict with the model’s parametric knowledge. Prior work studies these knowledge conflicts (Longpre et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2024) and encourages models to stay faithful to the given context (Zhou et al., 2023). However, following the context is useful only if it is true and applies to the question. In practice, context can fail either condition. It can be false, due to errors or misinformation in its source. It can also be true but out-of-scope, such as a retrieved passage about a similar entity or a different year, or a user document that does not match the exact question. In both cases, a model that faithfully follows the given context would end up answering the question incorrectly. We therefore refer to both types collectively as misleading context.

Misleading context. Most prior work on misleading context focuses on false context, which can override a model’s correct prior answer and impair question answering (Pan et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024). Other studies show that irrelevant context can distract models (Shi et al., 2023; Amiraz et al., 2025) and that passage order affects which evidence models use (Xie et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2024). Fewer studies examine true but out-of-scope context. RGB includes reports about other years, but tests them separately from false passages (Chen et al., 2024). Amiraz et al. (2025) test distracting passages with a gold passage in both orders, but without a matched false passage. TruthTrap studies truthful hints rather than retrieved context (Shafiei et al., 2026). None of these studies compares out-of-scope and false context directly. We pair the two per question so that both support the same wrong answer, and test each alone and with gold context in either order.

Scope in question answering. Several datasets study questions whose answers depend on scope. SituatedQA covers answers that change with time and location (Zhang and Choi, 2021), AmbigDocs covers distinct entities that share a name (Lee et al., 2024), and CondAmbigQA covers answers under explicit conditions (Li et al., 2025). RAMDocs further combines entity ambiguity with misinformation and noise (Wang et al., 2025). These datasets test whether models can find the answer for the right scope. We instead fix the target scope and test whether misleading context pulls models away from answers they already know. We build on SituatedQA and AmbigDocs to construct out-of-scope context and its matched false context.

3 MisleadQA

MisleadQA is a diagnostic dataset built to answer the two questions raised in §1: 1) whether out-of-scope context misleads models as much as false context, and 2) whether gold context prevents both errors. To this end, each item pairs a multiple-choice question with three kinds of context: gold context (G), true but out-of-scope context (S), and false but in-scope context (F). Each question has five options, including one for abstention. S and F support the same wrong answer, so their effects can be compared on the same question. The main split contains 959 items covering entity, time, and location mismatches, and a 25-item supplement on condition mismatches is analyzed separately (Table 3.2). Below, we formalize the design (§3.1), describe the sources (§3.2), and explain how we construct (§3.3) and validate (§3.4) the items.

3.1 Dataset Design

Questions and scopes. Each item contains a question qq that asks for the value of an attribute pp (e.g., minimum wage) at a target scope ss (e.g., California on January 1, 2015). A scope is a set of qualifiers, such as an entity, a time, and a location, that determine the answer. Let v⁡(⋅)v(\cdot) map each scope to the source-supported value of pp at that scope. The gold answer is y∗=v⁡(s)y^{*}=v(s). We also choose an alternative scope s′s^{\prime} (e.g., California on January 1, 2016) that changes exactly one qualifier of ss and keeps the others fixed. Its value ℓ=v⁡(s′)\ell=v(s^{\prime}) must differ from y∗y^{*}, and we call it the lure. Both values must be unique at the requested precision.

Contexts. Each context is a single claim c=⟨sc,vc⟩c=\langle s_{c},v_{c}\rangle with a stated scope scs_{c} and an asserted value vcv_{c}. It is true if vc=v⁡(sc)v_{c}=v(s_{c}), and in-scope if sc=ss_{c}=s. Each item has three contexts:

G\displaystyle\mathrm{G} =⟨s,y∗⟩\displaystyle=\langle s,y^{*}\rangle true, in-scope,\displaystyle\text{true, in-scope},
S\displaystyle\mathrm{S} =⟨s′,ℓ⟩\displaystyle=\langle s^{\prime},\ell\rangle true, out-of-scope,\displaystyle\text{true, out-of-scope},
F\displaystyle\mathrm{F} =⟨s,ℓ⟩\displaystyle=\langle s,\ell\rangle false, in-scope.\displaystyle\text{false, in-scope}.

Scopes are compared after normalizing years, jurisdictions, and entity identifiers. We exclude any S whose stated range covers ss, such as a time span that includes the target date.

Design rationale. S and F support the same lure but assign it to different scopes. They share the question, options, gold answer, and G (Figure 1), so F serves as a matched control for S, as in counterfactual-context settings (Longpre et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2024). The two also relate differently to G. G is consistent with S, because they concern different scopes, but it contradicts F. Adding G therefore tests whether models respond differently to the two kinds of misleading context. Since S and F differ in both truth and scope, their comparison reflects the joint effect of the two factors.

3.2 Data Sources

The main split draws on three sources, each covering one or two scope dimensions (Table 3.2). FRED is a public database of economic time series maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. We use its 44 annual minimum-wage series, which cover 43 states and the District of Columbia from 1990 to 2024. Because each value is tied to a specific state and date, we can change the time or the location while keeping the other fixed, and we construct questions that ask for a state’s basic minimum wage on a given date. SituatedQA (Zhang and Choi, 2021) provides natural questions whose answers depend on time or location, and we use it for time and location mismatches. AmbigDocs (Lee et al., 2024) provides Wikipedia documents about distinct entities that share a name, and we use it for entity mismatches. CondAmbigQA (Li et al., 2025) supplies the 25-item condition supplement. Items derived from the same jurisdiction or upstream question form a cluster, which we use for statistical inference (§4.3).
